1. **Fundamental theorem, second part, in $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be differentiable at every point of $[a,b]$ as
   a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]), and
   suppose $f' : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ is integrable. Then
   $$\int_a^b f' \;=\; f(b) - f(a).$$
2. **A bounded derivative gives a Lipschitz function.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable at
   every point of $(a,b)$, and let $M \ge 0$ satisfy
   $\lVert f'(t)\rVert_2 \le M$ for every $t \in (a,b)$. Then
   $$\lVert f(t) - f(s)\rVert_2 \;\le\; M\,|t-s| \qquad \text{for all } s,t \in [a,b],$$
   that is, $f$ is Lipschitz with constant $M$ as a map
   $([a,b], d_{\mathbb{R}}) \to (\mathbb{R}^{m}, d_2)$
   ([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]], [[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]],
   [[lem-metrics-on-rn]]).
Every continuous real function on a closed nondegenerate rectangle $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $m\ge1$, is Riemann integrable.

Let $A\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ and $B\subseteq\mathbb R^q$ be nondegenerate closed rectangles, and let $f:A\times B\to\mathbb R$ be Riemann integrable. Then the four lower and upper section-integral functions of [[def-sections-and-iterated-riemann-integrals]] are Riemann integrable and
$$\int_A\ell_B=\int_Au_B=\int_{A\times B}f=\int_B\ell_A=\int_Bu_A.$$

citations.quote: Let $K$ be a finite oriented three-dimensional cell complex with vertex, edge, face, and volume cochains. An edge cochain records oriented electric line integrals, a face cochain records oriented magnetic fluxes, and a vertex cochain records electric charge. Write $N_v,N_e,N_f,N_c$ for the retained vertex, edge, face, and cell counts. On a periodic cell, identify opposite cells with orientation preserved and let $G,C,D$ be the full vertex-to-edge gradient, edge-to-face curl, and face-to-cell divergence incidence matrices, each the transpose of its signed oriented boundary matrix. For a PEC closure, “interior” means not in the boundary subcomplex. Keep only interior electric edges as unknowns and only interior vertices as volume-charge locations, but keep all face fluxes, including boundary-normal magnetic fluxes, and all cells. This closure has no separate boundary surface-charge cochain. Define $G$ and $C$ by restricting the absolute vertex-edge and edge-face incidence matrices to those rows and columns. This mixed closure imposes zero tangential electric edge cochains on the boundary while allowing a fixed normal magnetic flux on boundary faces. In both cases, $G\in\mathbb R^{N_e\times N_v}$, $C\in\mathbb R^{N_f\times N_e}$, and $D\in\mathbb R^{N_c\times N_f}$ satisfy $CG=0$ and $DC=0$.

derivations.claim: On an oriented triangle with ordered vertices $[v_0,v_1,v_2]$, the coboundary of a vertex cochain $q$ evaluated on the triangle is its oriented edge sum $(q(v_1)-q(v_0))+(q(v_2)-q(v_1))+(q(v_0)-q(v_2))=0$. Hence each triangular face row of $CG$ vanishes. The same calculation is the transpose of $partial_1\partial_2=0$ under the incidence convention in [F1].

On an oriented tetrahedron, each edge in the boundary of its oriented boundary is obtained by deleting two different vertices. For each such pair of deleted indices, the two possible deletion orders have opposite signs, since $(-1)^i(-1)^{j-1}+(-1)^j(-1)^i=0$ for $i<j$. Thus every edge coefficient in the boundary-of-boundary is zero, so the cell row of $DC$ vanishes. This is the transpose of $\partial_2\partial_3=0$.

Periodic identification identifies faces with the prescribed orientation, so the quotient cell structure retains oriented boundary-of-boundary cancellation. For PEC, let $\bar G,\bar C,\bar D$ be the absolute incidence matrices and let $P_e$ select interior edges and $P_v$ select interior vertices. The matrices are $G=P_e\bar G P_v$, $C=\bar C P_e^T$, and $D=\bar D$. An interior vertex is incident to no boundary edge, so $P_e^TP_e\bar G P_v=\bar G P_v$. Hence $CG=\bar C\bar G P_v=0$, while $DC=\bar D\bar C P_e^T=0$. This retains boundary-face magnetic cochains although boundary electric edge values are fixed.

A positive definite square matrix has trivial kernel: if $(M_e+(\Delta t/2)S)x=0$, then its quadratic form at $x$ is zero and step 1.1 forces $x=0$. A linear map from a finite-dimensional space to itself with trivial kernel is bijective, so the solve exists uniquely for every right-hand side.

derivations.claim: The quotient defining $\lambda_{\max}$ is continuous on the compact set $\{e:e^TM_ee=1\}$, so the maximum exists and is finite. Also $e^TKe=(Ce)^TM_b(Ce)\ge0$, hence $\lambda_{\max}\ge0$. From the first row of [F2], $b^{n-1/2}=b_c^n+\Delta t Ce^n/2$ and $b^{n+1/2}=b_c^n-\Delta t Ce^n/2$. Expanding their $M_b$ inner product gives $\mathcal E^n=\frac12\|e^n\|_{M_e}^2+\frac12\|b_c^n\|_{M_b}^2-\frac{\Delta t^2}{8}\|Ce^n\|_{M_b}^2.$

Using [F2], the electric-energy increment is $\frac12\|e^{n+1}\|_{M_e}^2-\frac12\|e^n\|_{M_e}^2=\left(\frac{e^{n+1}+e^n}{2}\right)^TM_e(e^{n+1}-e^n)=\Delta t\left(\frac{e^{n+1}+e^n}{2}\right)^TC^TM_bb^{n+1/2}.$ The magnetic cross-energy increment is $\frac12(b^{n+1/2})^TM_b(b^{n+3/2}-b^{n-1/2})=-\Delta t\left(\frac{e^{n+1}+e^n}{2}\right)^TC^TM_bb^{n+1/2},$ by applying the Faraday row at times $n$ and $n+1$. The two increments cancel, proving conservation.

By the definition of $\lambda_{\max}$, $\|Ce^n\|_{M_b}^2=(e^n)^TKe^n\le\lambda_{\max}\|e^n\|_{M_e}^2$. Substitution into step 1.1 gives the stated lower bound. When $\Delta t^2\lambda_{\max}<4$, its electric coefficient is positive. If an admissible staggered state has zero energy, the bound forces $e^n=0$ and $b_c^n=0$; the Faraday row in [F2] then gives $b^{n+1/2}=b^{n-1/2}$, so $b_c^n=b^{n-1/2}=b^{n+1/2}=0$. Thus the energy is positive definite on update states.

Subtract the electric row in [F2] at indices $n$ and $n-1$, then use the magnetic row to replace $b^{n+1/2}-b^{n-1/2}$; this gives $M_e(e^{n+1}-2e^n+e^{n-1})+\Delta t^2Ke^n=0$. If $\Delta t^2\lambda_{\max}=4$, a maximizing vector $v$ satisfies $Kv=\lambda_{\max}M_ev$ by the constrained Rayleigh-quotient maximum. Thus $e^n=q_nv$ obeys $q_{n+1}-2q_n+q_{n-1}+\Delta t^2\lambda_{\max}q_n=0$, whose characteristic polynomial is $(r+1)^2$. Hence $q_n=(-1)^n(a+bn)$ is a solution and grows linearly when $b\ne0$. It is compatible with the full first-order rows by setting $b^{n+1/2}=(q_{n+1}-q_n)Cv/(\Delta t\lambda_{\max})$: the Ampere row follows from $Kv=\lambda_{\max}M_ev$, and the Faraday row follows from the scalar recurrence. For $\Delta t^2\lambda_{\max}>4$, the same recurrence has real reciprocal roots, one with modulus greater than one. This proves the endpoint caveat and instability above it.

derivations.claim: On a periodic Fourier mode, a forward edge difference in direction $j$ has multiplier $e^{i\theta_j}-1=2i e^{i\theta_j/2}\sin(\theta_j/2)$. The half-cell phase in the edge and face cochain locations is removed by a unitary diagonal change of Fourier basis, so the scaled directional symbol is $i d_j$ with $d_j=2\sin(\theta_j/2)/h_j$. The Cartesian curl symbol is therefore $i\boldsymbol d\times$.

The cross-product matrix $\boldsymbol d\times$ is real skew-symmetric. The identity $-(\boldsymbol d\times)^2=|\boldsymbol d|^2I-\boldsymbol d\boldsymbol d^T$ follows by expanding the vector triple product. Thus the curl-curl symbol is zero on the longitudinal vector $\boldsymbol d$ and equals $|\boldsymbol d|^2$ on its two-dimensional orthogonal complement. The Hodge weights in [F1] scale this eigenvalue by $c^2$, giving the stated $\lambda(\theta)$.

For a transverse mode $e^n=q^n v$ with this eigenvalue, subtracting the electric row in [F3] at consecutive time indices and using its magnetic row gives $q^{n+1}-2q^n+q^{n-1}+\Delta t^2\lambda(\theta)q^n=0$. Substitution of $q^n=e^{-i\omega n\Delta t}$ yields $4\sin^2(\omega\Delta t/2)=\Delta t^2\lambda(\theta)$, which is the displayed dispersion relation.

Since $0\le\sin^2(\theta_j/2)\le1$, $\lambda(\theta)\le4c^2(h_x^{-2}+h_y^{-2}+h_z^{-2})$. When every $N_j$ is even, the allowed tuple $\theta=(\pi,\pi,\pi)$ attains equality; otherwise the exact maximum is the maximum over the finite allowed tuples. Applying [F2] gives the rectangular strict bound and its cubic specialization, while preserving the finite-grid endpoint distinction.

In each material region the constitutive fields satisfy
$$\partial_t(\epsilon E)=\operatorname{curl}(\mu^{-1}B)-J_{\rm src}-\sigma E,\qquad \partial_t B+\operatorname{curl}E=0.$$
Here $J_{\rm src}$ is the impressed free-current density, while $\sigma E$ is the conductive current. Consider a homogeneous isotropic periodic Yee grid with $\epsilon,\mu>0$, wave speed $c=(\epsilon\mu)^{-1/2}$, spacings $h_x,h_y,h_z$, and $N_x,N_y,N_z$ cells. Its allowed wave angles are $\theta_j=2\pi m_j/N_j$. On a mode with wave vector $k_j=\theta_j/h_j$, the transverse curl-curl eigenvalue is
$$\lambda(\theta)=c^2\sum_{j\in\{x,y,z\}}\frac{4}{h_j^2}\sin^2\left(\frac{\theta_j}{2}\right),$$
and the lossless Yee leapfrog dispersion relation is
$$\sin^2\left(\frac{\omega\Delta t}{2}\right)=c^2\Delta t^2\sum_{j\in\{x,y,z\}}\frac{\sin^2(\theta_j/2)}{h_j^2}.$$
The exact finite-grid strict condition is $\Delta t^2\max_{\theta}\lambda(\theta)<4$, as in [[thm-maxwell-yee-strict-cfl-modified-energy]]. The rectangular sufficient bound is
$$\Delta t<\frac{1}{c\sqrt{h_x^{-2}+h_y^{-2}+h_z^{-2}}};$$
it is exact when every $N_j$ is even. For a cubic grid this bound is $\Delta t<h/(c\sqrt3)$. Odd cell counts may have a smaller finite-grid maximum, so the finite-grid eigenvalue is the exact criterion.

derivations.claim: For $\theta=(\pi,0,0)$, the sine-square sum is $1$, so $\sin^2(\omega_{\rm ax}\Delta t/2)=c^2\Delta t^2/h^2$. Its symbol direction is the $x$-axis, and $p=(0,1,0)$ is orthogonal to it, so this is a transverse mode.

For $\theta=(\pi,\pi,\pi)$, the sum is $3$ and $p=(1,-1,0)/\sqrt2$ is orthogonal to $(1,1,1)$. Thus $\sin^2(\omega_{\rm corner}\Delta t/2)=3c^2\Delta t^2/h^2$. The maximum eigenvalue is $12c^2/h^2$, so strict positivity requires $\Delta t<h/(c\sqrt3)$; equality places the maximal mode at the repeated-root endpoint.
